post.title: Why Every Agentic Pipeline Eventually Becomes a State Machine
post.content:
Three months into running a fully automated code-review pipeline, I watched it approve a pull request with a known security regression — not because the model was wrong about the code, but because the approval tool was a different process than the review tool, and they had silently fallen out of sync.

That kind of desynchronization is not a bug. It is the natural state of any agentic system built without explicit state management.

The industry is converging on "better models" as the solution to agentic failures. Prompt the model harder. Add more context. Fine-tune on failures. But the failures I keep seeing are not reasoning failures — they are plumbing failures. The model is fine. The pipe is broken.

## The plumbing I am describing

When I say plumbing, I mean the explicit, structured contracts between steps in an agentic workflow: what passes between stages, what invariants must hold, how the system recovers when a stage produces unexpected output.

Most agentic pipelines today look nothing like this. They look like a series of LLM calls with natural-language outputs connecting them. Stage 1 generates a JSON plan. Stage 2 reads that plan and writes code. Stage 3 reviews the code. The connections are implicit. The state is latent. And when any stage drifts — because the model is non-deterministic, because the upstream output format changed, because the tool's response schema shifted — the whole pipeline either fails loudly or, worse, continues silently with corrupted context.

The second case is the dangerous one. Loud failures are visible. Silent desynchronization is invisible until it reaches production.

## The formal plumbing I am describing

Each stage has a typed output contract. Not just "returns JSON" but "returns a list of objects with these exact fields and these value constraints." Transitions between stages are explicit: the orchestrator validates Stage 1's output against Stage 2's expected input before passing it along. Unrecognized fields are errors, not warnings. Unexpected types are errors, not coercion points.

This is not novel. This is how distributed systems have been built for decades. The novel part is that most AI engineering teams have not yet learned to apply these lessons — because until recently, the pipeline steps were not autonomous.

What changes when steps become autonomous is that the blast radius of a schema mismatch expands dramatically. A microservice returning the wrong field is a 503. An agentic pipeline silently approving a bad PR is a compromised production branch.

## Guardrails are structural, not reactive

I have seen the guardrails discussion frame agentic safety as "add a validation layer." That framing misses something important: guardrails are most effective when they are structural, not reactive.

A reactive guardrail checks the output of a step and rejects bad outputs. A structural guardrail changes the plumbing so that bad outputs cannot be generated, or if generated, cannot propagate.

The guardrails that have actually saved me — the ones that prevented silent failures — were not LLM-based content filters. They were schema validators at each pipeline boundary, plus explicit error states for every transition that was not "normal."

Reactive guardrails treat the model as the source of truth. Structural guardrails treat the protocol as the source of truth.

## The conclusion I keep arriving at

The bottleneck to reliable agentic systems is not model capability. It is engineering discipline around pipeline state.

This is unglamorous work. It does not get benchmarked. It does not ship with a new model card. But it is the difference between a pipeline that "works most of the time" and one that you would actually trust with production.

The best agentic systems I have seen look boring from the outside. They are well-structured, heavily validated, with explicit error handling at every boundary. They look boring because the interesting failures have been designed out.

That is the goal. Not an impressive demo — a boring, reliable system.
